title: Introduction to Data Science
text:
Collaborative Notes
The Fall 2026 collaborative notes supplement the instructor-authored Introduction to Data Science book. They give students practice explaining data-science concepts and working through a Git and GitHub review process.
The notes are maintained in the ids-f26 repository. Students contribute through topic branches and pull requests. The repository contains two kinds of presentation. A topic presentation explains a method or idea and belongs under topic/; a final-project presentation reports an original project and belongs under final/.
Each topic presentation needs a short catalog entry in its relevant topical chapter. Final-project presentations are collected in the Final Project Presentations chapter. In both cases, the slide deck is the substantive contribution; contributors do not need to rewrite slides as prose.
The topical chapters and final-project chapter organize and link to presentations; they do not duplicate the instructor book.

section: Clone and Render the Notes Locally
text:
Clone and Render the Notes Locally
Keep a local copy of these notes so that you can render presentations before opening a pull request. Place the ids-book and ids-f26 repositories in the same parent folder. If you plan to contribute, fork statds/ids-f26 on GitHub first, then clone your fork. Replace GitHub_Username below with your GitHub username:
cd path-to-your-course-work
git clone https://github.com/GitHub_Username/ids-f26.git
cd ids-f26
git remote add upstream https://github.com/statds/ids-f26.git
git remote -v
git status
If you only want a local copy for reading and rendering, clone the shared repository directly instead:
git clone https://github.com/statds/ids-f26.git
cd ids-f26
The book’s requirements.txt is the single source for course package versions. This repository’s requirements.txt includes ../ids-book/requirements.txt for the side-by-side checkout layout above. Follow the book setup instructions when creating the shared Python 3.12 environment for the first time.
Use the course Python environment that you already chose while working through the instructor book. Do not create another virtual environment or install packages inside ids-f26. From the ids-f26 repository, set ENVIRONMENT_DIRECTORY to that environment’s path and activate it:
ENVIRONMENT_DIRECTORY=/path/to/your/environment

# macOS or Linux
source "$ENVIRONMENT_DIRECTORY/bin/activate"

# Windows with Git Bash
source "$ENVIRONMENT_DIRECTORY/Scripts/activate"
To refresh packages after an approved dependency change, activate that environment and run make install from ids-book. If your checkouts are not side by side, use the actual book directory; the relative include above assumes the documented layout. Propose new dependencies to the instructor for inclusion in the book’s requirements rather than adding package pins here.
Confirm that the selected interpreter is the course environment before rendering:
python --version
which python
make check-tools
Render the notes and all accepted presentations with:
make render
Quarto writes the local site to _book/index.html. Open that file in a browser and inspect the page or slides before requesting review. While developing one presentation, render only that source file:
make render-one FILE=topic/last-name-topic/index.qmd
The _book/ directory is generated output and must stay out of commits. If a render fails because a package is missing, first verify the active interpreter and ask the instructor before adding a dependency to the shared course environment.

text:
Projects

Midterm
The midterm project uses hourly PM2.5 measurements to study air quality before and after congestion pricing. Submit completed work through Classroom 50.


Final Project
Begin considering final-project questions early in the semester. A suitable project starts with a meaningful question, uses data appropriate to that question, and communicates both findings and limitations. Potential sources of project ideas include:

ASA Data Challenge Expo
Kaggle
DrivenData
openFDA
Score Network
Paleobiology Database

[Add current milestones, deliverables, presentation requirements, and links to time-sensitive challenges.]


Final Presentation Peer Evaluation
Each student evaluates every other presenter using the same three criteria. Rate each criterion on a 5–1 scale, where 5 means excellent and 1 means poor. Do not evaluate your own presentation. Base each rating on evidence from the presentation and add a brief comment explaining the rating.
Use the following general scale:

5 – Excellent: exceptional, complete, and convincing;
4 – Strong: clear and effective, with only minor weaknesses;
3 – Adequate: generally satisfactory, but with noticeable gaps;
2 – Limited: partially successful, but with substantial weaknesses; and
1 – Poor: missing, seriously flawed, or not understandable.
Domain: Does the presentation motivate the work adequately? Does it explain what the project is for and why it matters? Does it place the project in context by reviewing relevant existing work appropriately?
Methods: Are the variables meaningfully constructed? Are the methods appropriate for the problem, and are they adapted effectively to the application? Are the computational methods used appropriately? Does the presentation acknowledge important limitations?
Presentation: Is the presentation clear, professional, and informative for a general audience? Are the findings interpreted effectively in nontechnical language? Do the tables and figures communicate the intended information clearly?

Topic Presentations
The private course syllabus contains the official assessment policies for topic presentations. This public chapter also provides the working rubric so that contributors understand what makes a strong presentation, pull request, and revision.

Topic Presentation Rubric
Topic presentations are worth 20 points. A topic presentation is a focused teaching contribution, not a final research project; original data, advanced methods, and novel findings are not required.

Approval and preview: 4 points. The topic is focused and appropriate, the proposed approach is approved, the preview is submitted on time, and the deck is sufficiently complete to review. Sources should be identified, and examples should run when computation is part of the presentation.
Oral presentation: 10 points. The presentation motivates the topic and explains its main idea accurately (3 points), develops a useful example and interprets its output correctly (3 points), discusses limitations, common mistakes, and specific takeaways (2 points), and uses readable slides with clear, organized, and engaging delivery (2 points).
Pull request and revision: 6 points. The source is organized, reproducible, and properly attributed (2 points); the contributor responds to review with a meaningful revision and maintains a focused pull request (2 points); and the final source and topical catalog entry are complete and correctly linked (2 points).

title: Introduction to Data Science
Introduction to Data Science
text:
Assignment Workflow
Graded work is submitted through the designated Classroom 50 repository, not through the instructor book or collaborative-notes repository.
Each assignment submission must use one .qmd source file that solves all assigned problems. Label every problem clearly inside that file so that the source and rendered PDF are easy to navigate. Use the homework template as the starting point for the required structure.
Follow the detailed Git workflow in Project Management, especially Exercise 2.7. That workflow explains how to inspect a repository, create a branch, stage named files, review diffs, write meaningful commits, inspect history, and preserve evidence of the work.
Fall 2026 assignment requirements are:

Accept the assignment through the course site and clone the resulting Classroom 50 repository.
Develop the single .qmd source file on a descriptive branch, solving all assigned problems and labeling them clearly.
Make at least ten small, meaningful commits for every assignment. Do not create empty commits or split meaningless changes merely to reach ten. Each commit should record a real development step and use an informative, imperative message.
Preserve the complete branch history. Record the branch name, commit hashes and messages, and concise command results in the assignment source or wherever the assignment specifies.
Before submission, activate the same Python virtual environment that successfully renders the IDS-F26 class notes. Do not create a separate homework environment or install packages into a different interpreter. From the assignment repository, verify the active interpreter and render the source file:
python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable); print(sys.version)"
quarto render your-homework.qmd
Record the interpreter path, Python version, render command, and successful result in the assignment source or required evidence. If the work needs a package unavailable in the class-notes environment, ask the instructor before adding a dependency. The grader will render the submitted source with an automated script in that shared environment, so matching the environment is part of the reproducibility check.
Push the branch and submit the .qmd source plus any required input files through the designated course workflow. A PDF is no longer required for submission; the grader will render the source. Do not submit generated output unless an assignment explicitly requests it.

The ten-commit requirement applies to each assignment repository, not to the semester notes repository as a whole. Graded assignments remain private in Classroom 50 and are not submitted as public pull requests unless an assignment specifically says otherwise.
Keep generated files out of the repository unless the assignment explicitly requests them. Use Git from the command line rather than GitHub’s file-upload interface, and never commit credentials or large data files.

title: 1  Midterm Project: PM2.5 and Congestion Pricing
text:
Exercises
New York City began charging most vehicles entering the Congestion Relief Zone (CRZ) on January 5, 2025. The CRZ covers Manhattan’s local streets and avenues south of and including 60th Street, with exemptions for the FDR Drive, West Side Highway/Route 9A, and connections from the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel to West Street (Metropolitan Transportation Authority 2024). Did the odds of a high-PM2.5 day at CRZ monitors change after the policy began, accounting for regional background conditions? We define a high day relative to the pre-policy CRZ data; this is a study-specific threshold, not a health standard.
This project builds on a published analysis of congestion pricing and air quality (Fraser et al. 2025) and extends its data through August 2026. Fraser et al. analyze continuous daily PM2.5 using prediction-based counterfactuals; the high-day outcome and segmented logistic model here are a separate course analysis, not the paper’s model. The analysis can show whether measurements changed around the policy date. It cannot, by itself, show that the toll caused a change. Weather, wildfire smoke, traffic, monitor operations, and other events can affect PM2.5 at the same time. Your report must separate the model’s estimated association from a causal conclusion.
Use the same virtual environment of the ids-book project to ensure reproducibility of your report on my computer.
You may use AI tools to brainstorm, explain data-science concepts and workflows, consult programming documentation, and suggest or debug code. You are responsible for running, checking, and understanding AI-suggested code; conducting the analysis; and writing your own interpretations and conclusions. Do not ask an AI tool to complete an exercise or produce your report. Disclose AI assistance using the statement in the report template.
Two ZIP files are provided, covering June 1, 2023, through August 31, 2026: NYCCAS data and AirNow data. Each ZIP contains one hourly CSV file. Keep both ZIPs in a local data/ folder next to your report. You may read the CSV files directly from the ZIPs or extract them first. Do not include the data files in your submission.
NYCCAS records are hourly averages, in micrograms per cubic meter, and the ObservationTimeUTC field explicitly identifies UTC. AirNow’s datetime field has no timezone offset in the CSV, but the AirNow hourly data specification reports observation times in GMT (UTC). In both files, a timestamp marks the beginning of its hour. The two files use different column names and formats. Read the source descriptions and inspect the files before deciding how to clean and combine them. AirNow may contain special or invalid concentration codes; determine how to handle them from the values and documentation. Do not treat a missing monitor reading as zero.
The data come from the NYC Community Air Survey (NYCCAS) archive (New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene 2026) and the AirNow API (United States Environmental Protection Agency 2026a). The AirNow hourly data specification documents its GMT timestamp convention (United States Environmental Protection Agency 2026b). NYCCAS readings are preliminary and its historical files can be revised. The accompanying data README explains which source snapshots contribute to each period and documents NYCCAS correction changes and records removed after sensor problems. Cite both data sources in your report.
Submission. Organize the report around these four steps. The project has 20 subquestions, worth 2 points each, for 40 points total. Include the Python code that produces every reported result, and explain each cleaning and modeling choice. Use ideas from chapters 1–9 of the course book: reproducible projects, data checks, preparation, EDA, visualization, and logistic-model interpretation.
Submit an independently written Quarto report to the Classroom 50 assignment. Include your source code, selected tables and figures, cleaning decisions, model output, and interpretation. Your report must run when the supplied ZIP files are placed in the expected local data/ folder. Do not submit the raw or cleaned data files.

title: 1  Midterm Project: PM2.5 and Congestion Pricing
text:
1.1 Inspect and clean the hourly source files.

State the observational unit in each file and identify the field that distinguishes monitors.
Identify each file’s timestamp and concentration fields, state the time zone and units, and explain what time an hourly timestamp represents.
Standardize the needed column names and parse timestamps as UTC. Report null-cell and duplicate monitor-hour counts. For each monitor, report the absent-hour count within its first-to-last observation window. Identify the monitor-month with the most absent hours, and distinguish absent hours from null cells and time before a monitor began reporting.
Inspect unusual AirNow values, including negative codes. Identify the invalid code or codes, report how many rows they affect, and explain the exclusion rule. Apply the rule to a working copy and leave the source files unchanged.
After excluding invalid codes, apply the paper’s strict range, \(0 < PM_{2.5} < 25.5\) µg/m³. For each source, report eligible, retained, and excluded row counts. Also report how many valid zero and high readings the rule removes, and explain why some high readings could be real events.



 1.2 Create daily data and merge the sources.

Create one monitor-day row for each NYCCAS and AirNow monitor with an observation that day. Calculate each row’s daily maximum and report the number of monitor-day rows for each source.
Average the available AirNow monitor maxima for each UTC date. Record the number of contributing monitors and report a frequency table of dates by number of contributing monitors.
Create dates from the UTC timestamps. Show one example hour whose New York local calendar date differs from its UTC date, and explain why the chosen date convention matters for a daily maximum.
Left-join the date-level background estimates to the NYCCAS monitor-day table. Report row counts before and after the join, validate the expected many-to-one join, and explain how dates without background measurements are represented. Do not join the hourly files directly or replace missing measurements with zero.
Create an indicator that switches on January 5, 2025, and an elapsed-days variable that is zero before and on that date. Retain January 2025 and report the indicator and elapsed-days values for January 4, 5, and 6.



 1.3 Explore and visualize the hourly and daily measurements.

Plot CRZ monitor daily maxima with month on the horizontal axis, daily maximum PM2.5 on the vertical axis, and a separate panel for each weekday.
Describe one seasonal pattern and compare two weekdays within a month, referring to the plot. Explain how the facets help make these patterns visible.
For each UTC date, average the available CRZ monitor daily maxima. Plot this series with the daily AirNow background series. Report the mean CRZ-minus-background difference before and after the policy date and the change in that mean difference. Explain why this raw contrast is descriptive.
Show frequency tables of dates by the number of contributing AirNow monitors and by the number of contributing CRZ sites. Explain why missing measurements are not zero-valued measurements.
Plot the daily CRZ-minus-background PM2.5 distributions before and after January 5, 2025. Compare their medians and spreads. Use a two-sided Mann–Whitney U test to compare the distributions: state the hypotheses, report both sample sizes, the test statistic and \(p\)-value, and interpret the result at the 0.05 level. Explain the test’s independence assumption and why seasonality and nearby-day dependence limit its interpretation.



 1.4 Model high-PM2.5 days and interpret the results.
For each UTC date, average the available CRZ monitor-specific daily maxima. Define a high day as a CRZ daily mean above its pre-policy 75th percentile. This study-specific cutoff is not a health standard.
Fit a segmented logistic model with time in years from the study start (\(t\)), an indicator for January 5, 2025, onward (\(T_t\)), years since that date set to zero beforehand (\(D_t\)), and daily AirNow background. Fraser et al. use square-rooted background; justify your chosen form. Other covariates, such as month or day type, are your choice. A general model is
\[
\log\left(\frac{P(H_t=1)}{1-P(H_t=1)}\right)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \beta_2 T_t + \beta_3 D_t + g(X_t),
\]
where \(H_t\) marks a high day and \(g(X_t)\) contains AirNow background and any other covariates. The coefficients \(\beta_2\) and \(\beta_3\) describe the immediate level change and the change in yearly trend, respectively.

Calculate the 75th percentile of the pre-policy CRZ daily means. State the resulting cutoff and define how it classifies each date as high or non-high.
Make a two-way cross-tabulation of high-day status by policy period (before versus after January 5, 2025). Show counts and percentages within each period. Also report the number of dates and summarize CRZ monitor coverage with a frequency table by number of contributing sites.
Fit the segmented logistic model. Report and interpret the intervention level-change and trend-change odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Explain your AirNow background term and any other covariates.
Plot observed high days and fitted probabilities over time. Also plot response residuals (observed indicator minus fitted probability) over time. Describe the pre-policy and post-policy patterns, whether the fitted change is an immediate shift, a trend change, or both, and any visible residual pattern.
Conclude by answering the research question. Use the residual pattern, dependence between nearby days, regional background, and possible confounding to explain how far the result supports a causal claim.

title: 2  Data Acquisition and Engineering
text:
Student presentations in this chapter concern obtaining, exchanging, storing, and programmatically accessing data.
Topic example: Working with an API
This example shows how to separate a documented data request from the analysis and how to avoid exposing credentials or depending unnecessarily on a live service.
Topic presentation: Accessing US Census Data by Amanda Noe
This presentation introduces Census data sources and demonstrates using the Census API in Python, loading an API key from a local .env file, and converting returned data into pandas data frames for plots and maps.

title: 3  Data Wrangling and Visualization
text:
3.1 Creating Presentations with Quarto
Student presentations in this chapter concern transforming, summarizing, and communicating data through tables and graphics.
Example presentation: Creating presentations with Quarto
This example introduces RevealJS presentations in Quarto, including slide structure, executable Python code, figures, and a pre-submission rendering check.
Presentation-skills example: Presentation skills for data science
This example focuses on clear stories, readable slides, effective delivery, and claims that are proportionate to the evidence.
Topic example: Reading a plot
This example demonstrates a focused explanation, a reproducible figure, and careful interpretation of association and causation.
Topic presentation: Data manipulation with pandas by Enrico Ong
This presentation uses FiveThirtyEight’s college majors data to show four pandas verbs: select, filter, create, and group. It ends by checking how many rows each summary used and what the result does not show.

title: 6  Final Project Presentations
text:
6.1 Example presentations
Final-project presentations report an original data-science project. They are different from topic presentations: a topic presentation teaches a method or idea, while a final-project presentation explains a question, data, analysis, evidence, limitations, and conclusions.
Each accepted presentation has its source in final/<project-name>/index.qmd. The rendered deck is linked below after the project is accepted.
These instructor-created examples demonstrate the expected project narrative.
